title: POC interop & tool-calling plan with Astragrid Systems
summary: Kickoff scoping for a 6-week POC to validate OpenAI-compatible integration and tool/function calling for Astragrid's internal search + orchestration layer. Discussed success criteria (latency, throughput, cost, structured output correctness), workload sizing (qps, token distribution), benchmark plan and timeline, SDK mapping and minor data residency/security constraints (VPC + KMS). Agreed next steps to exchange sample prompts, pilot config and schedule an initial benchmark run next week.

Tool/function calling and structured JSON outputs

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Cortez (Redwood SE), Sam Rios (Astragrid CTO), Jamal Li (Astragrid Lead ML Eng), Nina Torres (Astragrid PM)

Auto-summary (transcribed):
- 6-week pilot to validate OpenAI-compatible endpoints and tool-calling integration for Astragrid orchestration product.
- Focus metrics: P95 latency, end-to-end tool call correctness (JSON schema), throughput targets and cost envelope.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we did get the calendar invite out. Alex from Redwood here, I'm the AE on the account, with Priya and Daniel from SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:19] Sam Rios: Good, thanks Alex. Sam here, uh excited to figure out how Redwood plugs into our orchestration layer. Quick context: we run a search-plus-actions pipeline, so we'll be calling the model not just for text but to drive downstream tools.
[00:35] Jamal Li: Yeah hi all, Jamal — we want to test function/tool calling flows and make sure structured outputs match a schema we enforce, and also ensure latency at scale stays reasonable.
[00:46] Priya Shah: Great, that's exactly the focus. We'll scope the POC around three main axes: correctness of structured outputs, latency/throughput benchmarks, and cost/unit token economics.
[01:05] Nina Torres: And from product, we need clear acceptance criteria — what pass/fail looks like. For us it's: 1) >95% schema-conformant responses, 2) P95 tail under 350ms for 256-token avg responses, and 3) under X cost per 1M tokens — we'll surface the cost target after this call.
[01:32] Alex Morgan: Good, that helps. One thing to flag up front: Redwood offers both OpenAI-compatible endpoints and SDKs that map to function/tool-calling — so the integration can be nearly drop-in, or we can do the native SDK if you want tighter batching and caching.
[01:55] Jamal Li: Can you clarify what "OpenAI-compatible" means in practice? We have an internal SDK expecting completions/chat and a function-calling pattern.
[02:08] Daniel Cortez: Sure. Our API exposes OpenAI-style chat and completions endpoints; function calling follows the same schema where the model returns a JSON payload matching your function signature. The SDK also provides helpers for structured output validation and retry/backoff. Note that we have options for hosted, dedicated and private (VPC) deployments if you need data isolation.
[02:39] Sam Rios: We will likely need a VPC deployment or private plane (sic) — data residency is important for some of our customers. We are SOC 2 but we want KMS integration as well.
[02:53] Priya Shah: That's fine. For a POC we typically run on Redwood Hosted with a VPC peering / private endpoint or our Private control plane depending on timeline. For the benchmarks we can do a staged approach: hosted first for speed, then private if you want to validate the KMS/HSM flows.
[03:13] Jamal Li: Ok, let's talk workload sizing. Right now our production peak is roughly 90 qps across a mix of short (<64 token) and medium (~256 token) completions; worst-case bursts to 200 qps for a few minutes. Average response length is about 180 tokens.
[03:33] Priya Shah: That's super helpful. For benching we'll need a token distribution histogram and a representative prompt set. We'll test 1x, 2x, and 3x of your peak to see scaling behavior, and include continuous batching to measure tail latency.
[03:50] Alex Morgan: For success metrics — confirm we want P95 under 350ms for 256-token avg, and schema-conformance >95%. Is throughput target 200 qps burst-capable?
[04:07] Nina Torres: Yes, that's the bar. Also we want to measure cold-start vs warmed KV cache performance because many flows are interactive and cache behavior matters.
[04:18] Daniel Cortez: Right, Redwood's runtime handles KV cache and prefix caching; we'll instrument cache hit/miss. Note — sometimes transcriptions say K.V. cache, sorry — but it's KV cache, key-value cache for decoder states, which impacts latency.
[04:34] Jamal Li: On tool-calling: our orchestrator expects the model to return an exact JSON following our schema; small deviations break downstream parsers. Can Redwood validate and sanitize or do you expect us to run a post-parse layer?
[04:50] Priya Shah: We can do both. Our SDK can run schema enforcement client-side and we can configure the model to prefer the JSON output style (system message schema). For POC we'll test 1000 examples and compute percent-valid JSON. Also include fuzz tests for edge cases.
[05:10] Sam Rios: What's the typical failure mode? Are we more likely to see non-conformant JSON or hallucinated fields?
[05:18] Daniel Cortez: Both. Hallucinated fields happen when model is uncertain; non-JSON sometimes from punctuation. We mitigate with stronger system prompts, function signatures and post-parse validation. We'll capture example failures and triage.
[05:33] Alex Morgan: For the benchmark plan: Priya will run a set of runs on our curated model variants — we typically test base, quantized, and a latency-optimized variant. We'll track P50/P95/P99, CPU/GPU utilization, and cost per token.
[05:54] Priya Shah: And we'll include tool-calling specific tests: 1) single-step tool call, 2) multi-tool orchestrations, 3) nested tool args. We'll measure end-to-end latency including the downstream action invocation.
[06:12] Jamal Li: End-to-end: that means we need to simulate external services too, right? We can't hit prod systems during benching.
[06:20] Priya Shah: Correct — we can run a mock endpoint that simulates downstream service latency. Please provide a latency distribution you see in prod and we'll include that in the bench harness.
[06:31] Nina Torres: Timeline? If we start week of 4/13, what's realistic for the first benchmark?
[06:38] Alex Morgan: Proposed timeline: 4/12 Redwood sends pilot config and pricing; 4/13 Astragrid uploads prompts; 4/15 Redwood runs baseline benches (hosted) and shares results; 4/17 deep bench with tool-calling; 4/22 show results + decide on private deployment validation. So roughly a 6-week POC with milestones at 2 and 4 weeks.
[07:02] Sam Rios: That seems reasonable. Is the hosted bench data going to be stored? We need audit logs and ephemeral storage guarantees.
[07:09] Daniel Cortez: We keep logs per request and can configure retention — for POC default is 30 days unless you ask for shorter. For private deployments audit logs can be pushed to your SIEM via S3 or syslog. KMS integration is supported for key management.
[07:25] Jamal Li: Pricing: we'd like to understand the incremental cost to hit 200 qps bursts. Can you provide an estimate in the pilot config?
[07:33] Alex Morgan: Yes — the pilot config will include GPU sizing, predicted token throughput cost, and options for reserved burst capacity. We'll include a cost simulation for your token histogram.
[07:45] Speaker 1: [crosstalk] quick question on SDKs — do you support Python + Go?
[07:51] Priya Shah: Yes, official SDKs for Python, Node, and a Go client; plus OpenAPI client templates. The SDK has helpers for function-calling RPC style and structured output validators.
[08:05] Jamal Li: For our infra we prefer a drop-in OpenAI-compatible endpoint so we can avoid changing a lot of code. How different is that path from using Redwood SDK?
[08:15] Daniel Cortez: The OpenAI-compatible endpoints are nearly identical in API surface — same methods and function-calling signature. The difference is advanced features like automatic batching and prefix caching are easier to enable via our SDK, but you can use the OpenAI-compatible API and get pretty much the same behavior.
[08:33] Alex Morgan: Small note — some of the perf knobs (like continuous batching thresholds) are only configurable in the Dedicated/private runtime; hosted has safe defaults. We'll call that out in the pilot doc.
[08:47] Nina Torres: Any limitations on function size or number of tools? We have about 12 tool integrations we might call.
[08:55] Priya Shah: We support multiple tools; the main constraints are request payload size and the model's context window. We'll include guidance on best practices — multiplexing tool calls vs single large function payloads.
[09:10] Jamal Li: On the model variants — do you provide quantized models that are still OpenAI-compatible?
[09:18] Daniel Cortez: Yes, compatibility is preserved at the API layer. Internally we may run quantized kernels for performance. We'll show latency differences across variants in the bench report.
[09:29] Sam Rios: Security — confirm we can test KMS-wrapped keys in POC?
[09:36] Alex Morgan: For hosted we can do KMS integration for transit and envelope encryption; for a full KMS/HSM flow we might need Private control plane. We'll note this as a decision point after the initial bench.
[09:50] Nina Torres: Acceptance criteria again: >95% schema-conformant, P95 < 350ms, tool-call success rate >99% on mocked services.
[09:59] Priya Shah: We'll instrument those metrics and include dashboards. Also we'll produce an example failure-runbook for non-conformant outputs.
[10:10] Jamal Li: About telemetry — do you expose token-level cost per request so we can map to business metrics?
[10:18] Daniel Cortez: Yes, Redwood Console gives token-level breakdown and per-route cost and latency. We can provide access for your SREs during the POC.
[10:28] Alex Morgan: Ok let's go through the bench checklist fast: 1) sample prompts + token histogram (Astragrid), 2) mock downstream endpoints with latency distribution (Astragrid), 3) acceptance schema & test set (Astragrid), 4) Redwood to prepare pilot config + bench scripts (Redwood), 5) schedule run and review (both).
[10:50] Sam Rios: Sounds good. Any gotchas we should expect?
[10:53] Priya Shah: A couple: 1) function calling requires careful prompt design, sometimes you need a hard system message enforcing JSON; 2) prefix caching improves latency for similar prompts but can skew fresh prompt distribution results; 3) quantized models may slightly change output tokens, so check for tokenization mismatch in your validators.
[11:18] Jamal Li: For the JSON schema enforcement, can the SDK auto-correct small issues (like trailing commas) or do you strictly validate/fail?
[11:27] Daniel Cortez: SDK validator can attempt a best-effort fix and report confidence; for the POC we recommend both: attempt auto-fix and also track metrics where auto-fix was needed. We'll surface those in the report.
[11:40] Nina Torres: Who will be our point of contact for the bench run?
[11:44] Alex Morgan: Priya will run the bench and Daniel will help with the SDK/tooling. For commercial/pricing follow-ups that's me.
[11:52] Sam Rios: Ok. I want to call out our timeline constraint: we have an exec review on 5/20 and would like initial results by 5/8 to prep slides. Is that doable?
[12:03] Alex Morgan: Yes that maps to the 6-week timeline; we'll prioritize results and a summary report by 5/8.
[12:11] Jamal Li: Quick technical — do you support structured output testing against JSON Schema Draft 7?
[12:17] Priya Shah: Yes we support Draft 4/6/7 in the validator. We'll include the schema runner in the bench harness.
[12:26] Speaker 2: [laughs] ok that's a relief.
[12:30] Alex Morgan: Next up, any legal/procurement blockers for POC? Usually a simple MSA + data processing addendum suffices. For VPC/private we might need an SOW.
[12:42] Sam Rios: Procurement might need a short SOW. I'll flag that to Nina.
[12:47] Nina Torres: I'll coordinate.
[12:50] Priya Shah: We'll attach a short pilot SOW and default security pack with SOC2 docs.
[12:58] Jamal Li: On metrics instrumentation — we want per-request traces so we can map model latency with our orchestration steps.
[13:06] Daniel Cortez: We can pass request IDs and provide tracing hooks/headers for correlation with your traces.
[13:12] Alex Morgan: Ok, let's confirm deliverables and owners one more time.
[13:16] Alex Morgan: Redwood: pilot config + pricing (Alex), bench scripts + run (Priya), SDK examples (Daniel). Astragrid: sample prompts + token histogram (Jamal), backend mock latencies and acceptance criteria (Nina/Sam).
[13:33] Sam Rios: That matches our internal notes.
[13:36] Nina Torres: We'll aim to get the sample data to you by 4/13.
[13:41] Alex Morgan: Perfect. We'll tentatively schedule the bench for the 17th — Priya will follow up with a calendar invite.
[13:49] Priya Shah: Yep will do.
[13:52] Jamal Li: One small detail — tool-calling side effects. If the model triggers actions we need idempotency guarantees during bench. Can we configure a dry-run mode?
[14:03] Daniel Cortez: Yes — the bench harness will simulate calls and can run in a dry-run mode returning simulated success codes. We'll log what would have been executed.
[14:12] Nina Torres: Great. Any other questions?
[14:16] [pause — several people typing]
[14:30] Sam Rios: Not from me. Thanks for the clarity.
[14:33] Alex Morgan: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the pilot doc and pricing later today.
[14:39] Jamal Li: Thanks.
[14:41] Priya Shah: Thanks everyone.
[14:43] Daniel Cortez: Bye.

(Transcript continues with brief Q&A and wrap; timestamps above are approximate — some short cross-talk and mis-heard words present in auto-transcription.)
